title: A Galaxy Adrift
caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 1398, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope
celestial: NGC 1398 · constellation Fornax · about 65 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: Dark Energy Survey/DOE/FNAL/DECam/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA. Image processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), J. Miller (Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab), M. Zamani & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: NGC 1398 shows off a bright central bar and delicate spiral arms, a barred spiral galaxy that seems to drift alone in a field of stars. Its home on the sky is the constellation Fornax, roughly 65 million light-years from Earth.
A closer look shows that the galaxy is far from alone. The sky around it is full of the smudges and swirls of distant galaxies, far beyond NGC 1398.

In a barred spiral, a straight band of stars crosses the center, and the spiral arms begin near its ends. Deep images like this one, covering a wide field, let astronomers study one galaxy in detail while also recording huge numbers of much more distant galaxies at the same time.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (25.20 x 18.00 arcminutes) and distance (65 million light years), the frame spans roughly 476,000 × 340,000 light-years. Its light set out about 65 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: The Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope observed NGC 1398 through g, r and i filters, covering visible and near-infrared light. The colors assigned to each filter are not published.
filters: 486 nm · Optical g (NSF Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope DECam)

understand.eye: The distant background galaxies are far too faint for the eye. The survey's deep exposures reveal them, and the i filter reaches into near-infrared light.

explore: The image was taken with Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory's Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope. In 1995 the telescope was named in honor of Víctor Manuel Blanco, a Puerto Rican astronomer who became the observatory's second director. It was captured for the DOE-funded Dark Energy Survey using DECam, built and tested at Fermilab.
alt: A barred spiral galaxy with a bright bar and delicate arms, surrounded by stars and many small, faint distant galaxies.
